title: Saudi Court Overturns Death Sentence Over Deleted Facebook Comment
excerpt: Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan worker Anojan Sivarasa, 27, but whether he still faces prison or can return home remains unclear.
body:
• Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan migrant worker Anojan Sivarasa, 27, on 13 October, Sri Lanka's government said.
  • Sivarasa was first given five years in prison and a 3 million riyal (about $800,000) fine over a deleted Facebook comment, before an appeal court imposed death in September.
  • It is not yet clear whether the prison sentence stands, whether he remains in detention, or when he can return home; his family says a further hearing is expected on 17 October.
  • Sri Lanka's president and deputy foreign minister thanked Saudi authorities, while Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International had urged that his life be spared.

Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence imposed on Anojan Sivarasa, a 27-year-old Sri Lankan migrant worker convicted over a Facebook comment, Sri Lanka's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra announced on Wednesday 14 October. The ruling was delivered on 13 October, two days after lawyers filed the Supreme Court appeal, according to Asia Daily's detailed account of the case.

Sivarasa is no longer under a death sentence. What happens next is still unresolved: whether his earlier prison term and fine stand, whether his conviction itself has been quashed, and how long he remains in Saudi custody have not been made public.

How a deleted comment became a capital case

The case began in late June, after footage circulated online showing a dog that had followed Hindu pilgrims being kicked near Kalmunai in eastern Sri Lanka. The video triggered heated religious arguments on social media.

During one exchange, after another user reportedly posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, Sivarasa responded in Tamil with a comment insulting the Prophet Muhammad. He deleted the comment and posted a video apology. A screenshot nevertheless reached his employer in Saudi Arabia and Saudi authorities, and he was arrested in July, as reported by The Insight International.

Sivarasa, a Tamil man from Narpittimunai near Kalmunai who had travelled to Saudi Arabia for construction work in September 2025, told a judge he wrote the comment in anger and later expressed remorse, Amnesty International said. Amnesty also said he had no access to a lawyer between his arrest and his first sentencing.

From five years to death, then a reversal

The Al-Ahsa Criminal Court first sentenced Sivarasa to five years in prison and a fine of three million Saudi riyals, about $800,000, under the Anti-Cybercrime Law. Prosecutors appealed. On 17 September, an appeal court in the Eastern Region increased the sentence to death.

Colombo responded on two tracks. Sri Lanka sent a legal delegation to work with Saudi lawyers, and officials pursued the case diplomatically. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake met Sivarasa's family and assured them the government would keep working to save him. The Supreme Court appeal was filed on 11 October.

After the reversal, Dissanayake welcomed the decision and promised continued help until the remaining proceedings end. Hemachandra thanked Saudi authorities and the legal teams of both countries. Sri Lankan lawmaker Faizer Mustapha, who was involved in the legal effort, told BBC Sinhala the team was reviewing the ruling.

The Saudi position and the rights criticism

No Saudi government statement on the Supreme Court's reasoning had been published in the reports available at the time of writing, and the full ruling has not been made public. The outcome was announced by Sri Lanka, not by Riyadh. What is known from the court record reported so far is the sequence: a cybercrime sentence first, a death sentence on appeal under the appeal court's interpretation of Islamic law, and then a Supreme Court decision setting that death sentence aside.

Human rights groups had pressed the opposite case on principle. Human Rights Watch urged Saudi Arabia to stop handing out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offences, especially against migrant workers. Amnesty International called for Sivarasa's conviction to be overturned and for him to be released.

"No one should be imprisoned, let alone face execution simply for expressing their views."

— Amnesty International, as reported by Asia Daily

What happens next

Sivarasa's family, who said they had no direct contact with him after 28 September, say a further hearing is expected on 17 October. That hearing may clarify whether he still faces prison, whether he can leave Saudi Arabia, and when he might return to Sri Lanka.

For the hundreds of thousands of South Asian migrant workers in the Gulf, the case is a stark reminder that a post made in a home-country argument can be judged under the law of the country where they work — and that consular and legal help, when it arrives early, can change the outcome.

items.event: Sivarasa posts the Facebook comment during an online argument, then deletes it and apologises.
Sivarasa is arrested in Saudi Arabia.
Al-Ahsa Criminal Court sentences him to five years in prison and a 3 million riyal fine.
Appeal court increases the sentence to death.
Lawyers file the Supreme Court appeal.
Supreme Court sets aside the death sentence.
